messages.subject: Re: checkpoint vs packrat
messages.body_plain:
Hi Paolo,
checkpoint is a more comprehensive package from a reproduction standpoint. This is because it works in tandem with a server side solution, the checkpoint-server. Most of the burden is on the checkpoint-server, not the end user. Packrat does not have a concept of client or server, and a user could still find themselves in "dependency hell". Packrat requires a user to rsync, scp, or some how get your Packrat file and code to another user. That can be a cumbersome and tedious process.
With checkpoint package, all you need to reference in your code is the snapshot date, and then you can commit your R code to a public or private repository, such as github.com <http://github.com>. Then all another user has to do is pull your R code down, run it, and they will be using the same packages as you, because they are using the same snapshot date.

In short, the checkpoint-server brings order to the world of R packages. It knows exactly how things looked at a given point in time, and everyone sees the same stuff, therefore everyone is on the same playing field.

For more information please review this page:
http://projects.revolutionanalytics.com/documents/rrt/rrtpkgs/

Chris Mosetick
Revolution Analytics

messages.subject_clean: clarification about co-existence of RRO and "CRAN R"
messages.body_plain:
So, RRO is supposed to be fully compatible with R, in some sense of the meaning of compatible... which is what I would like to ask to find out more about.

My main concern is that installing it will wreak havoc on my current R installation(s) (from ubuntu 14.04 packages or RHEL 6.6 packages), and in turn potentially with R + RStudio setup.

The installation webpage present the possibility of installing RRO side-yb-side with another R installation, and my understanding is that in the end it boils down to replacing the "R" executable, which is a script, with a different one that sets things up to use RRO.
That seems easy and manageable enough.
However, reading the few posts on this group immediately raises the concern that in fact things may not be so smooth.
Judging by the content of the deb package, RRO files may go in their own tree.   That said, I am a little puzzled by the absence in the package of something that may by the 'R' executable (there is a Rscript file, but no actual R script).

So, my first question is for some slightly more articulated overview of how RRO installs itself, and what may be the collision points with existing installations.
If the only overlap are R and Rscript, I guess it's easy enough to make backup copies of those installed by the base packages.
At a higher level, if somebody wanted the side-by-side installations to be both usable, what would be the easiest way of achieving it?

Assuming the main R installations are not getting on each other's way, there remains an very important and thorny issue: "user installed" package (I am very worried that that's where the shit will hit the fan!)
How does RRO handles them?
I guess there are two main scenarios:
1. Does it re-use whatever has been installed and it finds in the default R_LIBS_USER?
2. Does it want me to reinstall them, placing them in a different location in a way that will not interfere with the functioning of "CRAN R"?

Case 2. may actually be more desirable, except for the nuisance of re-installing a ton of packages, because my understanding is that when installing a package R is actually compiling it from source code and I presume that doing it while running RRO will result in better performing user-installed packages.  Case 1 may work, because RRO and CRAN-R are probably binary compatible, but the performance of the packages is less likely to improve (if it can improve at all... perhaps some dynamic linking would enable that).

If RRO wants/can install packages from scratch, how can the user control this and make sure to (a) not mess up the packages installed by the other-R, (b) make RRO and other-R use their respective libraries?
I guess it may be simply a matter of careful/clever managing of environment variables and stuff like that...

I understand that these questions may be beyond the scope of your support for RRO, but I will claim that they are very likely extremely common among people who would like to give RRO a shot and in many cases the uncertainty about them would prevent from trying.
I have been on the fence for weeks and I won't probably step down without some clarifications because I don't want to mess things up... although the worst case scenario is probably cleaning the slate and re-install, that is not zero-work/zero-headache...

I hope you will have a chance to address these questions and perhaps put together a slightly more extended "README" for installing RRO side-by-side with another R.

Thanks a lot.

-GF

messages.subject: Re: [RRO] Using foreach with RRO
messages.body_plain:
Hi Bob,

MKL and doMC shouldn't interfere with each other, but it might not be a good *idea* to use them both together. In your example, both MKL and foreach will be contending for CPU resources on all available cores, which might not be optimally efficient. It depends on how CPU-intensive the MKL operation and the foreach operation are. It's worth trying setMKLthreads(1) to restrict MKL to a single thread when using foreach to see if that improves performance.

Using foreach and MKL together should never cause the R engine to hang, though. doMC can have some unexpected interactions when you use R with a GUI, though. Are you using R from the command line, or from RStudio or Eclipse or anything like that? Can you try running your code directly from the command line (without a GUI or IDE) and see if the hang still occurs?

Thanks,

messages.subject: Re: docker for RRO?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Enzo,
I saw your comment in Github as well. I'll respond here for now. RRO targets Ubuntu, not Debian. I am a huge Debian fan, but we have chosen Ubuntu for RRO because of the predictable release schedule.

We have RRO running on a Ubuntu 14.04 container. The Dockerfile that the automated builds use is based upon the rocker Debian unstable Dockerfiles. (I make sure to mention that in the code comments.)

You can find the RRO on Ubuntu container info here:
https://registry.hub.docker.com/u/revolutionanalytics/rro-ubuntu/

to get started using it:
docker pull revolutionanalytics/rro-ubuntu

Create a directory on your local system inside your home directory, Rdata for example, then use that as a place to analyze your data with the containerized RRO like so:

docker run -v $HOME/Rdata:/data -it revolutionanalytics/rro-ubuntu R

Where /data is the location inside the container to point your analysis to.

More formal usage notes will follow in the future, but this should get you started. Please feel free to provide feedback here if you have any comments, questions or issues.

As for the layering that you mentioned, we might do something similar in the future.

Chris Mosetick
Revolution Analytics

Changing the settings to "--vanilla" lead RRO to act in batch mode.  With this setting all is OK: I see the cursor, I can use the console as a normal REPL. The issue is that ANY error terminates the session (and this is correct for R working in batch mode).    As I do MANY errors this is very annoying and defeating the purpose.

My hypothesis is that RRO either ignores or misbehaves when the directives  "--interactive", "--no-readline" are set (not relative to batch mode).

Would it be possible to "test" these functions to make sure that all is OK with RRO?

Many thanks

messages.body_plain:
Hi, Giovanni

I use Windows, day-to-day and can assure you that on Windows the installation is entirely side-by-side:
The R executable sits in an entirely different folder
The user libraries are entirely separate
But we update the path, so that the R executable in the RRO folder becomes the default R installation
>From time to time I use Ubuntu to test RRO, and my experience and understanding is that on Linux this works in a very similar way:
The R executable sits in an entirely different folder
Again, the user libraries are entirely separate
On Linux we overwrite the path variable.  So to refer to your previous R installation, you need to explicitly know the path
Note that on MAC OSX it's different - only one installation of R can live inside the Framework, unless you make some relatively advanced changes yourself.

I hope this helps.

Andrie

Visit mran.revolutionanalytics.com/open <http://mran.revolutionanalytics.com/open> for information
